children.value: The agent migration benchmark measures whether a coding agent resolves a real lifecycle finding, and whether the finding's
changes that outcome. It runs every task twice — once from a bare task prompt and once from the packet prompt — in separate worktrees at the task's pinned commit.

This page publishes the task set, the two arms, the scoring rules, and the reproduction commands. It deliberately contains no estimated numbers: the measured per-agent results are not recorded in this repository yet.
A measured run needs real agent hosts and local clones of the pinned repositories. It is tracked separately in
, which will publish the per-agent tables and link them here.

, path, and line) that a scan of that commit reports, an expected end state, at least one verification command, and the real migration commit used as evidence.
The expected end state is checked with regular expressions over the named files: each
must be present. The verification commands are the project's own build or test commands, such as

The task title, rule id, and finding location, with an instruction to make the smallest change and run the verification commands. No packet.

A fresh offline scan of the worktree must report the same rule at the same path and line. The harness then builds the finding's migration packet (affected files and usages, constraints, pinned runtimes, and verification commands) and renders it as the agent prompt.
Both prompts are written to a temporary file outside the worktree and its path is exported as

For each arm the harness records the agent exit code, wall-clock duration, diff and changed files, the expected-end-state checks, and every verification command's exit code and duration. A condition is unsuccessful when the agent exits non-zero, a check fails, verification fails, or the run errors (for example, when the fresh scan does not report the finding).

The allowed set is the finding path, every expected-end-state check path, optional caller-supplied related paths (typically the packet's affected files), and companion lockfiles next to those paths (

Rates are fractions of attempts: success rate, finding-resolved rate, verification-passed rate, and no-unrelated-changes rate, rounded to four decimal places.

When real runs exist, each row will record the agent and its version, the model and its version, the arm, attempts, successes, success rate, and the three criteria's counts and rates. Runs are not filtered: every failure and timeout is published with the row. The fake adapters used by the tests exercise the harness offline; they are not measurements, and CI never calls a model.
Requires Node.js 22 or newer, network access to clone the pinned repositories, and the toolchains the tasks verify with (Rust, Go, Docker, .NET, PHP, Ruby, Node.js, Bun, and Yarn as applicable).

npm ci
npm run build --silent

# List the task ids.
node dist/benchmarks/agent-migrations/run.js --list

# Clone one pinned repository, then run both arms with a real agent.
git clone https://github.com/sharkdp/hyperfine ~/src/hyperfine
node dist/benchmarks/agent-migrations/run.js \
  --task hyperfine-atty \
  --repository ~/src/hyperfine \
  --agent-name claude-code \
  --agent-command 'my-agent "$OFFING_MIGRATION_PROMPT_FILE"' \
  --output artifacts/agent-migrations/hyperfine-atty-claude-code.json

# One arm only, with explicit timeouts.
node dist/benchmarks/agent-migrations/run.js \
  --task hyperfine-atty \
  --repository ~/src/hyperfine \
  --condition packet \
  --agent-name claude-code \
  --agent-command 'my-agent "$OFFING_MIGRATION_PROMPT_FILE"' \
  --timeout-ms 1800000 \
  --verification-timeout-ms 1800000

The agent staleness benchmark measures how often coding agents write end-of-life or deprecated choices when they produce common project files — Dockerfiles, GitHub Actions workflows, Kubernetes manifests, package manifests, Terraform modules, and small Python or Node helpers — and whether Offing's agent hook changes that rate.
Each task is a version-free prompt that names only the file to write. The harness runs every task twice in a fresh temporary directory: once with no Offing setup (
). The produced file is saved under
that records the agent version and date. Scoring is offline:
and reports, per agent, arm, and category, the share of tasks with at least one finding, findings per task, and the rule ids seen.

to generate 200 TypeScript files in a temporary repository and scan them as one batch. Every file contains one aliased package import, one real method call, one comment lookalike, and one string lookalike.

The benchmark expects 400 true usages. It reports detected usages, precision, recall, and wall-clock scan time, and exits unsuccessfully unless precision and recall are both 1.0. The time is observational rather than a fixed CI gate because filesystem and runner performance vary.

On 2026-10-14, the benchmark detected all 400 usages with 1.0 precision and 1.0 recall in 29.64 ms on the development machine. Treat the duration as a reference point, not a cross-machine performance guarantee.
The same command also compares the two usage engines on the repository's own

(120 files, real code, no network). The regex scanner runs as one batch over the directory; the tree-sitter analyzer parses and queries each file. Each engine runs 15 times after a warm-up, with a contract of Node.js file-system and path imports and calls, and the report gives the median and 95th percentile of a whole-corpus run. The first tree-sitter run also loads the WebAssembly runtime and grammar, so it is reported separately as

Tree-sitter took about 4.9 times as long at the median, roughly 1.1 ms per file, in exchange for finding multi-line calls, aliases and re-exports and rejecting method calls that only share a name with an import (see
). The figures are reference points, not a CI gate.

The benchmark corpus is intentionally controlled. The automated test suite separately covers JavaScript and TypeScript import forms, aliases, Python imports and calls, configuration keys, ignored dependency directories, and comment/string false positives.

) scans a clean temporary copy of the fixture in-process with the built-in detectors, scan caches disabled, and no network access. It runs one warm-up scan, then three measured runs, and reports the mean wall-clock time and the peak resident set size of the process. A scan that reports no findings also fails the gate, so a broken-but-fast scan cannot pass.
Mean wall time over the measured runs

Both budgets carry roughly an order of magnitude of margin over the reference measurement so that runner noise never trips the gate — only a deliberate or catastrophic slowdown does. Raise a budget in the same commit that intentionally regresses scans, state the reason in that commit, and update this table; the ceilings live in
The same job also protects each detector's speed.
scans a clean copy of the committed fixture corpus (
, every ecosystem side by side) with one detector at a time, caches off, and compares each detector's median wall time over five scans with its ceiling in
. A slow change fails with the detector's name:
::error::detector ruby: median scan time 1900 ms exceeded the 1250 ms budget

Ceilings are eight times the median measured over repeated local runs, with a 750 ms floor, so runner noise does not trip them. A detector over its ceiling is measured up to two more times and fails only when its best median is still over. Every built-in detector must have a ceiling and every ceiling must name a built-in detector, so a new detector cannot ship unbudgeted.
